utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, as a result of some significant development, it's necessary that I apply for a change of witness order, and I would seek your leave to address you further on the matter in the first place in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: These are the four witnesses who we'll deal with by way of Rule 92 bis applications now. They are C-1050, 1129, 1194, and 1065. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, in relation to them we have, I should say, the amici observations on them. The first of them, 1050 or, rather -- yes, 1050, this was a witness who heard about the disappearance of several victims. He is related to some of the victims who are referred to in the indictment, and he gives evidence about their disappearance, but I think he can give no more evidence than to say that he saw them one day and then they disappeared. Is that about right?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And he's actually someone who simply states that they were taken away by Arkan or Arkan's men, and he does not make reference to other perpetrator groups. And having the previous decisions of the Trial Chamber, I think this is the one candidate where we could say it could be a 92 bis without cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The other three, 1129, 1194, and 1065 deal with Erdut. In the case of 1129, she saw the arrest of people, identifies the sorts of uniforms, and tried to -- tried to find them. It involves also a count in the indictment, so it is submitted, paragraph 53. 1194 was involved in the siege of Vukovar. He gives direct evidence about the involvement of the JNA in the siege. And 1065, he was arrested by Martic's Police and beaten and later held in the prison. The amici suggest that the evidence isn't cumulative, and what your answer to that would be, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have quite a different answer for this person because we do not want to call him any more. We have seen this person --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You don't want to call him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No. We have seen this person and he is of very fragile health and hardly able to come here, so we decided to drop this person altogether.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. So that is 1065.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. And for the -- in relation to 1194, there is a lot of references and involvement of the JNA and its structures, and we think, therefore, this witness should be cross-examined; equally the other one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 1094 should be cross-examined.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And 1129. There's also the involvement of the JNA in these arrests.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: However, Your Honours, you may consider whether in relation to 1129 the cross-examination should be shorter than the usual hour because it's very, very little reference to the JNA. Otherwise, it's just a relative of victims who saw them being arrested and taken away and, later, the bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Mr. Kay, is there anything you want to add to what's in your pleading?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No. We've put in detailed submissions which I know the Trial Chamber has and has already referred to, so there's no need for repetition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, anything you want to add to the argument about these - now it's three - witnesses under Rule 92 bis?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll consider these applications. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is another matter in relation to the switch of witnesses. We actually consider the witness -- one witness for whom we just filed a protective measures motion yesterday of -- which you should have a courtesy copy, and if this witness would be called today, the decision on these protective measures should be made first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which -- which number is that, so we have it, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: 1230, C-1230, and requested protective measures --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We've had that motion. We will grant protective measures in the terms asked.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we come to the first of the 92 bis witnesses to be dealt with this week, may I make a general observation about them and preface it in this way: Having no participating lawyers for the accused, the accused indeed taking almost no part in procedural debate, it's sometimes quite difficult for us to express our opinions as strongly as we can when we have vigorous opponents in court and Judges simply deciding between arguments, though if we express ourselves too fiercely or sometimes strongly it looks as though we're seeking conflict with another part of the court, which we're not. With that observation and with the usual moderation and, I hope, decorum that I hope characterises all our procedural observations, we would press the Chamber in respect of 92 bis witnesses here for cross-examination to consider carefully the amount of time that the accused has for cross-examination. And I'd like to remind the Chamber, if I may, of what appears on page 17 of the long witness list. I've got the relevant part recopied and Ms. Dicklich can distribute it or put it on the overhead projector. I've already lost my -- This chart, if it can be made available to you again or possibly thrown on the overhead projector, it's non-contentious. For those familiar with the way computers work, it can come as no surprise to know that this is a chart that arithmetically corrects itself as matters are brought up-to-date, and the Chamber may recall looking at it at the middle or foot of page 17, and the Chamber will understand that what it seeks to do is to show that as of the date of the chart - it's probably changed a bit since then - the total number of days required for our witnesses on the list, 92 bis apart, would be some 83. And then the total number of days required for 92 bis for Croatia and for Bosnia would be respectively 12.5 and 25, leading to the total number of days of 120 so that we've got to find somewhere cuts of 37.5 days. That's the way the chart works.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: May I interrupt you with something.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think your mathematics may be out when you claim to have 83 days left from the 24th of June. I may be wrong about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If it's less, then our dilemma -- not our dilemma, our problem is greater, and we must obviously correct that, and we would be grateful for any information that can be provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I make it that you will have 80 days left then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: From that date?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll investigate that. But, Your Honour, the position is this, and this is why I show the chart: The 92 bis requirements or needs that we perceive are premised on each 92 bis witness taking an hour in toto. That we hope not optimistic calculation was built on the 45-minute cross-examination allowed in the latter part of the Kosovo trial and reflecting that counsel who will be taking these witnesses, Mr. McKeon, later Mr. Whiting and Mr. Saxon, will deal with the presentation of the witness in just a couple of minutes, I hope never more than five save in absolutely exceptional circumstances. Now, once the accused is allowed and if he takes an hour and if there's material from the amici, the time taken is dramatically more than that hour or significantly more, it comes up to an hour and a quarter and all too easily an hour and a half, and this chart will reveal that if the figures of 12 and 25 have to be increased via the 25 per cent or 50 per cent, the reality is we're going to be losing several - somewhere between seven and 15 - witnesses who provide evidence of the other and perhaps more valuable kind to the Chamber, and therefore the chart shows in a dramatic way the impact on the case we can present of the time taken by the accused in cross-examination. And I observe that the first 92 bis witness dealt with in this way last week was dealt with by the accused, in our respectful submission, by the last five minutes being absolutely relevant to the issue in hand, where he accused the witness of making up the entire story and had some kind of positive case to put to him. The first 55 minutes or 50 minutes having been taken up by material to which the witness was in large part quite unable to give responsive answers, and the Chamber may remember at some stage that he pleaded that the accused should ask him questions about what he was there to help with and not about matters that he couldn't help with. And we would invite the Chamber simply to be as alert as it always is and as mindful of the consequences of the accused simply wasting time with these witnesses when it considers whether the amount of time available for cross-examination of a particular witness or in general should be as much as an hour or less. As I say, without an articulating lawyer representing an accused, it's sometimes difficult for us to put our arguments with the manifest strength that we would wish, but we do urge this on the Chamber as a matter of great importance, and the chart shows why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is a matter very much for the Trial Chamber and our discretion. To shut the accused up would be wrong, in my view, to prevent him cross-examining properly. Of course we have in mind, more, if I may say, than the problems the Prosecution may have in getting their evidence in, the necessity that time is not wasted. That is a real consideration. But we must allow the accused the opportunity to cross-examine and put his case. He is entitled to that, but we'll have in mind what you say, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I'm very glad that the Presiding Judge spoke because I'm very offended by your submissions. Try as you might, I think it's an oblique criticism of the manner in which the Trial Chamber has been conducting the case. We have established guidelines and we follow the guidelines. What we are dealing with here is essentially a question of fairness, which cannot be reduced, in my view, to mathematical and statistical calculations. We have in mind all that you have said, and I consider this submission to have been entirely unnecessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm very sorry that Your Honour takes that view, and if I may say so, I entirely and respectfully disagree with Your Honour's position. I go back to what I said at the beginning: It is actually very difficult with an accused who is not represented to press our points with the vigour that we think they merit, and I have been at all times been extremely cautious in my approach to the Chamber in expressing views which may run counter to the perceived view, as we perceive it, of the Chamber. I've done it cautiously, respectfully, and well understanding, if I may say so, the absolute need of the Chamber to be seen to be conducting a trial that is fair the accused. On the other hand, if we reach the position of holding the view that the Chamber should be respectfully reminded of its ability to limit cross-examination that is to no useful effect, it is our duty to the Prosecution to make that position clear. If there was a lawyer representing the accused, as I said at the beginning, and it's why I said it, we can explain our position in an adversarial setting that allows us to express our opinions strongly with there being no suggestion of criticism of the Judges, because there is no suggestion of criticism of the Judges in what I said. Not at all. Nevertheless, if we want to draw to your attention the consequence of the accused wasting time, if that is what he does, then we must do that. Where Your Honour says to me it's not a matter of arithmetic, I again respectfully differ. You didn't put it in those terms, but I rephrase it. There are two ways in which it is a matter of calculation. The Chamber has said that there is a rule of thumb to be applied in the amount of cross-examination to be allowed. We have from the beginning respectfully said we understand that but that we would urge cross-examination to be allowed on a merit basis. That remains our position. And the second point is this chart does show that if more than an hour -- if an hour is taken as opposed to, say, half an hour or 45 minutes, for cross-examination of 92 bis witnesses who may have limited value to the evidence pointing directly to this accused, then the Chamber will inevitably have less witnesses of the kind who can point directly to the accused. That is something we have to present to the Chamber. But it's not done with any intent to be offensive to the Chamber. Far from it. And the suggestion that I would ever take such a course is one that I absolutely reject. I have addressed this Chamber on every occasion with the decorum and respect that is appropriate, and I'm not going to change.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Our next witness would be Witness C-006. This is a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, while the witness is being brought, I would like to tender an exhibit, and that's the 92 bis -- Rule 92 bis statement of Witness Yvonne Milewski. Her statement was allowed without cross-examination. I would like to -- tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If the registry could deal with it conveniently.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, Prosecution Exhibit 477.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And are copies available for us?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It would be helpful if we could have all these 92 bis witnesses and the transcript witnesses as early as possible. I don't know what proceedings are going on to get the declarations taken, but the sooner we have them, the better.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And it's all under way. It will come in very soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, the witness please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If the witness would take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this witness C-006?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is the witness. We've seen already he's taken the declaration. We need --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've got the wrong witness, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You've been brought in by mistake. Would you mind waiting outside. We're going to call another witness first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McKeon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. You've been granted certain protective measures by the Trial Chamber, and this morning we'll refer to you by your pseudonym C-006 during the course of these proceedings. I'd like to ask that the pseudonym sheet be placed in front of you, and I'd like you to take a look at that and answer by yes or no whether that is your name on the first line of the document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Sir, now, to further protect your identity, we've listed in the third line the surname by which you used to be known at the time of the events you will be testifying about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: And for the Court, the circumstances for the changing of his surname are described in the written statement in paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: At any time during your testimony if you need to refer to your former surname, with leave of Court, could you just say, "My former surname," and the Chamber will know what name you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Also, Your Honour will see that on the pseudonym sheet there's a list of four names, and next to the name, it says person A, B, C, and then it says "my father."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: With the Court's permission, I would ask, if you need to refer to any of these names, that you refer to them as Person A, Person B, Person C, and again the Court will know who you're speaking about.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Now, C-006, in recent days did you have an opportunity to go over your witness statement in the presence of an officer of the court and attest to its accuracy, subject to any corrections that you noted, and did you sign that documentation showing that you had attested your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: I'd like to offer the statement of C-006 into evidence under Rule 92 bis under seal as a protected witness, Your Honour. We also have prepared a redacted copy of the statement which can be made publicly available that takes out his identifying information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to summarise what the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's get an exhibit number first.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 478.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to summarise this witness's testimony. In October of 1991, as a young man of mixed Serb-Croat background, he was forcibly taken to Vukovar from Sid, Serbia, where he was questioned about his loyalties. During this questioning he was hit.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel, slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: The witness was eventually released after being held prisoner for two nights. After his release, he was given a uniform of the Serb Territorial Defence in Vukovar. After the fall of Vukovar on 18 November 1991, the witness went to the Velepromet in Vukovar to try to find a relative. While there, he heard people being threatened with being slaughtered because they were all Ustasha, and he saw prisoners being hit. The next day, in the late morning or early afternoon, the witness went to the Vukovar Hospital. He saw the hospital surrounded by JNA military police who were controlling access, and he also saw Major Sljivancanin standing in the yard of the Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would counsel slow down for the interpreters, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Major Sljivancanin was pointed out as the one who was in command of the JNA in Vukovar. From the hospital, the witness went to the Velepromet on the 19th. He saw there buses and trucks arriving filled with people. Some people were dragged off the buses and identified as Ustasha simply because they were wearing yellow Borovo boots which for some reason had been associated with Croatian fighters. On the morning of 20 November 1991, the witness was at the house of a friend, and while there a woman started yelling that they were taking the Croats out of Vukovar and that no one was going to prosecute them. The witness got into a car and drove to the Velepromet with a friend who wanted to check to see what was happening. He was told the Croats were taken to the JNA barracks, so he went there and saw nothing. He left and returned about 30 minutes later, and the scene had changed dramatically. Five to six buses had arrived, and Major Sljivancanin was there. Civilian cars started arriving with Territorial Defence soldiers and reservists. Among these men were Stanko Vujanovic and Miroljub Vujovic. As soon as they arrived, they got into what appeared to be a heated argument with JNA officers, including Major Sljivancanin. The witness saw brothers, the Dosen brothers, found on the buses and taken off and beaten so badly that it appeared they were on the verge of death. The brothers were placed in a white van with others and driven away. The witness saw there were a large number of JNA soldiers at the barracks, most of them military police. The JNA also had several tanks and APCs parked nearby, and these appeared to be manned by their crews. In contrast, there were few Territorial Defence soldiers there, and they were clearly outnumbered by the JNA soldiers. The buses eventually left, escorted by two to three military vehicles like jeeps. Military police remained on the buses when they left. The witness made inquiry and found out the buses were going to Ovcara, so he went there. When he got to Ovcara, he saw men being taken from the buses one by one and made to run through a gauntlet of soldiers who beat them as they passed toward a hangar. The witness was told by someone to watch a rear door of the hangar to make sure no one escaped, which he did for a short period of time. He then walked back to the front of the hangar where he saw several JNA officers, including Major Sljivancanin, and he saw a pile of suitcases and another pile that had personal items in it, including identification documents. The witness went into the hangar where several prisoners were being held. Behind a rope at one end of the hanger were approximately 20 men identified to him as specially trained criminals, and among them was one woman that he saw. In the rest of the hangar, men were seated along the walls and on the floor. Also there, he saw Miroljub Vujovic and Stanko Vujanovic, who appeared to be in charge. The witness saw that some of the prisoners were released from the barracks when people signed for them. The witness stayed at Ovcara for only a short period of time after that, and then he left when it was dark outside. Within three days of these events, within three days of 20 November 1991, the people in Vukovar were already speaking openly about what had happened at Ovcara and the fact that all the prisoners that he saw there had been killed. Thank you, Your Honour. We turn the prisoner -- the witness over for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is attached to the statement, Mr. McKeon, is that right, three hand-drawn maps of the various locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. Those maps were drawn by the witness at the time that he signed his original statement and they are part of his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. This is a case where the evidence is such that it seems to me that an hour is an appropriate time rather than less as the Prosecution were asking earlier. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness C-006, you come from a mixed marriage, your father being a Croat and your mother being a Serb. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The name and surname of your father is as written in tab 1, at the end of that tab, in the list; is that right? Is that your father's full name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is your father alive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When the events took place that you're testifying about, that is to say in 1991, did he live in Vukovar or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: I don't know. My parents divorced when I was about a year old. I never saw him in my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he has nothing to do with the events in fact and is no part of your testimony actually?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Your mother, after she divorced, married a man for whom you say in your statement, in paragraph 3 -- actually, you give his nickname in paragraph 3; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: Sorry, would you mind repeating the question? I didn't quite understand the translation. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, as in paragraph 3 of your statement, I understood this to be the nickname of the man your mother married later on, but I see in tab 1, on the other hand, that that is your nickname. So whose nickname is it listed in tab 1?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before you -- before you answer, you should have a copy of these various documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. You're talking about article 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, paragraph 3. From that I understood that it said your mother had married a man whose nickname was the one listed in tab 1 as being your nickname. So whose nickname is it in tab 1; yours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: It is my nickname and his last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. It's a surname. It's the last name of the man your mother married, your stepfather's, in fact, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Is your stepfather a Croat by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: He's Hungarian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 3 of your statement, you say that after 1991, you legally adopted your mother's maiden name. I'm not going to mention your father's surname for your protection. And you say that because it was a distinctly Croatian name and often caused you problems; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Can I request anything? Sorry. Is it possible for me not to listen to English translation? I understand perfectly what he's saying. This is just getting me confused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The usher will be able to arrange things there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, let's see how we get on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would you repeat the question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 3 of your statement, you say that after 1991, in a legal manner, you say you legally adopted your mother's maiden name in view of the fact that your father's surname - and I'm not going to read it out for your protection although it's written here - was a distinctly Croatian surname, and as you say, it often caused you problems; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What problems did you have because of your father's surname? You said that you had many problems, or often problems.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what problems were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: [In English] As a Croat, I've been -- people would approach me and just give me those looks. What am I -- in the sense of what am I doing here. And stuff like that basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But did anybody mistreat you because of it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: No, because basically I had a protection of a friend of mine that I was living at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And your name is as it says here now, and that was the name you took, your mother's maiden name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please pause between question and answer, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're being asked by the interpreters to pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to remember what date it was when you changed your surname?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was it after the fall of Vukovar, before the fall of Vukovar? Do you have any idea?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: After Vukovar fell, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have a document proving you had the surname you changed later on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... with me, but do I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you do have the birth certificate and all the other necessary certificates?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And all that is recorded in the registrars in Vukovar, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is another complaint. Could you remember, Witness C-006, it's difficult to bear it in mind, but there is a problem of interpretation. So allow the accused to finish and pause so the interpreter can interpret the question, and then answer. I know it's difficult, but could you try and remember.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will, sir. Thank you. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you've been living abroad for some time now -- I assume, Mr. May, that I'm not supposed to mention the country; right? -- and that can be seen from the English version of your statement, tell me, please, do you have the passport of the country you're living in today or do you hold a different passport or, rather, my question to you is whose national are you? You are a citizen of which country?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. We'll go into private session to deal with these matters.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. C-006, in paragraph 5 of your statement, you say that in January, 1991, when you went on leave after you'd been doing your military service, that you and your friends who were soldiers, that you had some problems with the -- with Croatian -- some Croatian policemen but that there was no violence --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you wait, Witness C-006. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how many friends of yours went on leave with you? I don't want to ask you their names, not to have to go back into private session, but how many of you were there who had gone on leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: There was three of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what were you by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The other two, what was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you're not sure, then I'm sure the question of their ethnicity was not the subject of your problems with the Croatian police --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- it wasn't why you had those problems. You just had problems because you were soldiers; is that it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just tell me now, please, as briefly as possible, what were these unpleasantnesses and problems you had with the Croatian police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: First they stopped us, they asked for identification, which wasn't the usual process, that civilian police ask military to show IDs. Then we'd been called names. We were told that we don't exist as the army, what are we doing here, where do we live? They've taken our identification cards. They wrote something in their books. They kept us over there, I would guess, about half an hour, still calling us names and stuff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the only reason for that was because you were in JNA uniforms; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In that same paragraph, you go on to say that when you arrived home that same evening and when you went to bed, that you had a far greater problem from the policemen, caused by the policemen, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Than the one you had with the policemen. At about 1.00 a.m., as you yourself say, in your family home, four men stormed the place. They pulled you, dragged you out of bed, and took you to a place called Sotin where they proceeded to abuse you practically the whole night. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that they kept calling you a Chetnik throughout that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And I assume they only called you that because you were a soldier.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: I don't know how to answer that question. Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you describe to us briefly, please, how they mistreated you and how long it went on for.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: Basically, they drove me over there. Even in the car they were beating us -- me. Sorry. And they took me out of the car, kicking me and yelling at me, showing me the paper that says over there that my signed statement, that my death sentence. They were kicking me still. They made me sign the paper where all has been said, and then made me eat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Despite the fact that, as you say, they were masked, did you manage to recognise any of these people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: No. They were all in civilian clothes and wearing masks on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you able to make any conclusions as to the fact that they belonged to any organisation in view of the fact that they had dragged you out of bed, called you a Chetnik, beat you, mistreated you, made you sign a statement, a document, and then made you eat it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: No, I guess not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: These masked attackers, was it obvious that they were some kind of Croatian extremists?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question. I don't really know. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From the injuries they inflicted on you that night, you spent almost a month in hospital, is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... around 20 days, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And after that, you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: And I returned --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- didn't have to do your military service any more?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: -- I returned to Ljubljana and after a couple days spent in hospital over there, I was released from duty, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I wanted to establish. Now tell me this, please: Do you have any consequences of the injuries and beatings that you were exposed to, today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: No, no. Bruises all over my body. Mostly my upper body.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So as far as I understand it, that has nothing to do with the decision taken to release you from continuing your military service; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: No. I was changed that I suffered so many stressful -- I was suffering so much stress and I was practically begging to get out of the army, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Up until then, as far as I am able to gather, since they called you Chetnik, you had had problems because they considered you to be a Serb; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: I would say yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But until then, you had no problems because you wore a Croatian surname before you changed it --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- is that right? But then, nevertheless, you changed your surname even though you didn't have problems because you had a Croatian surname.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether I was clear enough. You had problems because you were considered a Serb, and you were mistreated on those grounds and called a Chetnik, but you changed your surname, though it was a Croatian surname and it hadn't caused you any problems; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Anyone. Did you have problems with anyone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: Before the war or after the war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. C-006, the interpreters and court reporters have difficulty in understanding you, so could you please put a pause between the question and answer. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us not waste any more time on this. Is this true that your family, in the course of 1991, received anonymous and threatening telephone calls harassing your stepfather because he, as stated here in paragraph 6 of your statement, had married a Chetnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Only because your mother was a Serb; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Your mother, as far as I understand it, had absolutely nothing to do with any activities, if I can call them that, that could have been considered offensive or insulting towards Croats. She had married a Croat, and in every respect she was a normal citizen.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Her only fault was her nationality, the fact that she was a Serb; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Of course a fault, when I say a fault, I use it in quotation marks in the context --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- of these events. Tell me, please, did you ever establish who was behind these calls, these threatening calls?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: No. There were so many calls coming almost every day. Not only to us. We heard a lot of other people -- people have been called and threatened and stuff, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That brings me to my next question, actually. So there was such threatening calls to inhabitants who had any kinship relationships with the Serbs to bring pressure on them, is that right, who were related in any way to Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: I would say that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And was that pressure designed to force you to leave, to move out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: I don't know, but I guess they just wanted to scare us. Yes, I guess. I'm not really sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So because of everything that happened to you, as you have described these threatening calls because of the ethnicity of your mother, in July 1991 were forced to leave Vukovar --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- is that right? Tell me, where did you move to? Where did you find shelter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: We went to Belgrade as refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you fled under pressure because of the Serbian origins of your mother.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You fled to Belgrade. You were shortly followed by your stepfather who was a Croat; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: He's Hungarian, but yes. Yes, he came after us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. He came after you. Yes. You said he was Hungarian. Did he have any problems in Belgrade because he wasn't a Serb?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So not only you, but your whole family, in 1991, had problems exclusively because of the Serbian origins --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: I would say so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- of your mother? Do you know anything about the problems encountered by Serb families in the region of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: I can only say that I -- I did heard -- I did hear a lot of rumours going around, but nothing that I can confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever learn or do you know today the full name of a certain Miroljub?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether this should be asked in private session, because it is linked to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the 4th of November --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let us go into private session to be on the safe side.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the truck they transported you in there were some other men, judging by paragraph 8 of your statement; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know them? Were they people of your age, from the same place as you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: As far as I understood from the conversation that I -- the short, brief conversation that I had with them, they were from Vukovar. No, I didn't know them, and they were not my age. They were much, much older than me. I would say around 40s.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But they were given the same treatment as you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: No. They were not taken -- they were not put in a truck with me together. They were already in the truck when they put me in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But they treated you the same as they did them, I assume?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understand from your statement that they wouldn't let you talk and that there were two soldiers, reservists, guarding the truck, who were wearing beards; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: Yes, there were a lot of people wearing beard at the time, but yes, those two were wearing a beard, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: However, though you were not supposed to speak in the presence of those two bearded reservists, you somehow managed to learn that the others had been in prison in Sremska Mitrovica. Is that what you said? Or does this apply to only one of them? I wasn't quite able to understand what exactly you meant.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... all around us, basically, and a truck stopped. Those two guards came off the truck. That's when I had a brief chance to talk to them. One of the guys addressed me, actually, and he said what am I in for, and I said I don't know. And he said he's coming from Mitrovica, he's basically -- he was a prisoner over there for a while, charged by -- for rape in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: For rape in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know the name or at least the nickname of any of the people who were with you on the truck on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understand that they drove you someplace and, as it was dark, you couldn't tell where you were, but you realised soon that you were within the compound of the Velepromet company in Vukovar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I assume you established that as you were from Vukovar and you were familiar with the surroundings when you got off the truck.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: You could hear people saying, but, yes, I did recognise the building, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And before that, had you been within that company's compound?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: Yes, many -- many times before the war, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's a commercial company, I assume, since its name is Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: It's actually a big warehouse, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Of a commercial company; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you were only 19 at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That evening, you were interrogated by a person that you established was the father of this person that is the second name in tab number 1; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that person on that day had brought you there; right? That same man. Not the one who was interrogating you but this person named here, is that right, under number 2?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: No. He didn't come with us, no. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That evening -- let me just check something, please. You say here in paragraph 10 - that is why I wanted to clear this up and that is why I'm asking you this - "Then that same man took me to an office where an older man was seated, also in uniform. This man's name was --" and I won't mention the name -- "but it was only later that I found out that he was the father of the man who had abducted me in Sid. He began asking me how I had got there, and I explained what had happened in Sid." So the father of the person that had abducted you that same day. You just said it wasn't correct. Maybe something's wrong in this statement, or is what I just read out right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: The man who was in Sid, he stayed in Sid, but yes, this is the father of the man who, yes, took me out of Sid. Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then this man who stayed in Sid, he's the man who abducted you; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: Yeah. He brought me to the house, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He just brought you to the house.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: That's what's said -- that's what's said in my statement. Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But you explained that he didn't kidnap you, he invited you to go there. He suggested you go to a coffee bar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then you go on to say that that evening a man beat you, and you learnt that he was the bodyguard of a certain Miroljub Vujovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you learn the name of that man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: No, but I saw him a couple of times with him, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who is this Miroljub Vujovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: I later learned that he was a commander of the TO in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Two days later, a man saved you who you say was a friend of your parents. We don't have his name on the list here, but I assume I shouldn't read out his name either. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: If you want to, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He took you to his home where, in addition to the members of his family, there were some other people.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume the names of those people are not confidential, Mr. May, because they're not on this list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll go into private session and we'll consider the matter there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We don't need a private session. I won't go into that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll go on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It takes too much time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there were some people there and you mention them in paragraph 14. One of them was from Kosovo and you say he came to fight in Vukovar, but you don't know his name; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where did this man who saved you, your parents' friend, where did he live?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: Petrova Gora. That's a part of Vukovar. Yeah. That's part of Vukovar, yeah. Name -- place -- place called Petrova Gora, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And these other two men that I asked you a moment ago with reference to paragraph 14, and without reading out their names, were they also locals from Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: Those two names -- except that Kosovar guy, yes, they were Vukovar. They were both from Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 16 you explain that after about a week you decided to write a letter to your mother and that you mailed it or, rather, you sent it via one of these two men who were in the house who were citizens of Vukovar who was able to travel normally to Belgrade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, why didn't you do so through the man who saved you, who was friendly towards you? And it seemed to me logical that a man who saves you should be the one to take your message to your family?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: He [Previous translation continues]... he wouldn't go to Belgrade. That was my chance because this certain person was travelling that day to Belgrade, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In paragraph 18, you explain that on the 18th of November, with that same man that you mention as your saviour, you went to Velepromet to try and find your grandmother; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: Both of them, grandmother and grandfather, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this man who saved you was also a Serb, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, why were you looking for them in Velepromet? Why did it occur to you to look for them there, to look for your grandparents there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: Whoever came out of -- out of the basement during the war or after Vukovar fell, they were all gathered over there, questioned, and then sent wherever they -- wherever they felt like, basically. So that was the first logical place to look for them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the people who came out of basements were interrogated over there and then released; is that right? To go where they wanted to go; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And those were your father's parents, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: No, my mother's side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. Your mother's parents.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I assume they were Serb since your mother was Serb.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: My grandfather is a -- well, he's a stepfather of my mom's. Yeah, he's a Croat and my grandmother is Serb, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 21 you describe that in the night between the 18th and the 19th of November, in the house of this man who saved you and that you name in paragraph 13, the man whose name you didn't know, the man from Kosovo, arrived. And on that day, he boasted of having mistreated Croats, and he spoke about some sort of Chetnik Serbia. Is that how you explain it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And after a violent argument with this man, he took out a hand grenade, pulled out the pin, intending to blow you all up, as you say, because you disagreed with his behaviour and with what he was saying; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: Yes. They disagreed with the whole thing, yes. That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I got the interpretation that they agreed but you said disagreed, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: They disagreed in their conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You and the other people who were present were against that, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did that man seem to be in his right mind or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... I don't know. I can't make a judgement on that. He was -- he was full of stories that he was doing all kinds of stuff, and I'm -- I can't judge that. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, since you speak about these two men who were with you there, these two Serbs who argued and struggled with this man to prevent the hand grenade from blowing up, there was a kind of fight?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... they managed to get him on the ground and take it from him, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, why was that man in that house at all? How come he was there at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: Well, there were a lot of people coming in and getting out of the house. And any day -- day or night. It doesn't matter what time it was, people would just come by and maybe have a drink or go out, and stuff like that, yeah, so he just sort of dropped by.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was a private home, a private house, as far as I understand. It wasn't a coffee bar or anything like that. People just dropped in. Were they neighbours or what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: Yes, it was a private house, but the real owner wasn't over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And these people had been living there for some time, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: Well, they were over there when I was brought in, so I guess. I can't say for sure. I'm not sure. I'm not sure about the time line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The next day, on the 19th of November, 1991, as you state in paragraph 22 of your statement, while you were alone, you were unexpectedly interviewed by a Serb --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- TV journalist; is that right? You say that she was dissatisfied when she heard your surname. Did she ask you that at the beginning or at the end of the interview?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: At the end of the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember which TV station she was from? Do you know her name, at least?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: No, I don't recall, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember what she asked you during the interview?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: I remember exactly what she said, because she asked me my opinion, what happened over there, and at the end of the interview she asked me if I can say my name, and that was it. That's all I remember from that, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a convenient moment to adjourn. Witness C-006, we're going to adjourn now for 20 minutes. Could you remember not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that does include the members of the Prosecution team. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How much more time do I have, Mr. May?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me tell you. You've got 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I'll try and get through this as quickly as possible. I'm going to skip the interview, the interrogation -- the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you said that you assumed it wasn't broadcast because of your surname; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... pardon me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that why you changed your surname?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: No, for some other reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And you claim that on that morning, in the yard of a house, that you noticed some bodies lying down on the ground.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you considered that these were people who had died in hospital but weren't able to be buried because of the shelling, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: We were told that -- by the guards at the hospital that all those people are from the hospital, but we don't know -- I didn't know at that time who are -- why are they in the yard of that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And were they the bodies of Serbs or Croats? Did you manage to establish that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: I guess later on the identification was done by authorities, but not at that time, I didn't know who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That same morning, you say that you saw in the hospital a man who they pointed to as being the commander of the JNA forces in Vukovar and that you later learnt that he was Major Sljivancanin; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And on the basis of everything you said, following from your statement, everything you saw during the few days that you spent in Vukovar, I gain the impression that you moved around Vukovar quite a bit. Is that right? Did you go together with this man Zoric?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: Yes. I was walking with him, yes. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where he is now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: He's dead. He died in a car crash after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He was a Serb, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did he have a functional position of some kind in Vukovar? Because I gain the impression that in the general chaos that reigned there, he was some sort of influential person. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: No. He was a -- he was just a regular TO soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he was a soldier of the Territorial Defence, is that it? And you went with him as a civilian; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: Yes. He was in TO; and no, I wasn't a civilian, I was in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me this: Why did he as a soldier of the Territorial Defence, why was he looking for his father and mother in the Velepromet hangar, which is in paragraph 24 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: When they left Vukovar, I guess when the war started, they were left behind and they stayed in the basement. And as far as he understood, they were either killed - that's what he believed - or they were taken to Velepromet among the other people that were coming out of the cellars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And as far as your grandmother and grandfather are concerned, they left, as far as I understand it, through Serbia, Bosnia, and went to Croatia; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: Yes. They were brought to Velepromet. They were both questioned. They were searched. Everything was taken from them. They were taken to Sremska Mitrovica to gaol where my mother took them out. Actually, she took my -- my grandmother. My grandfather stayed in gaol for another certain time, amount of time, and he was exchanged as a war prisoner for -- I don't know exactly when, but, yes, they left for Zagreb after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then on the 19th of November, while you were waiting for Zoric at Velepromet who was looking for his parents, you saw the buses bringing in people into the area, into the compound; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say that on that occasion the local Serbs accused individual people of being Ustashas and set them apart as such. Is that what you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: People were brought in buses and trucks onto Velepromet. They were taken out, they were separated. Women and children were taken on one side, the men were taken on the other side, and yes, there were a lot of pointing of fingers on people and people called Ustashas and separated from women and children, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, all right. But in that second sentence of that same paragraph, in paragraph 25, you state and I quote: "All the men were made to stand in a column while the soldiers were trying to establish who was a Croat and who was a Serb." So I'm asking, did the local Serbs know who was a Croat and who was a Serb, who was who?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: When people are coming from -- from basements, they're all yellowish, no colour in their faces. People are coming in all -- they were dressed in really badly manner. Yes, they were lined up, they were asked their names. And no, I guess not everybody knew names of all the people that were coming out of the basements. So I guess you cannot know everybody, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And Zoric on that particular day, as you say in paragraph 27, managed to set five Croats free; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: That's true. As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How was he able to have them released? Can you explain that? And do you know the names of any of those people who were released on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: I don't recall any names. They were all his friends. Basically he was a passionate hunter, and he knew a lot of people. He was at the middle age at that time, like I would say 45, and they were all his friends. So the way he did it is I guess he just spoke to whoever was in charge over there to let them go. Because for a lot of people it was just a matter of seeing somebody -- sorry. It was just a matter of knowing somebody to basically take them out from there if you're sort of --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You say that on the 20th of November, as you say in paragraph 28, Zoric took you to the JNA barracks because he was afraid that in the group of people who was there he would find some of his friends; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why did he stop looking for his parents, then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: He finally heard that they're alive and well in Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you went back to the barracks with Zoric, you mentioned that you saw some jeeps coming with Stanko Vujanovic and Miro Vujic in them. You say that in paragraph 31, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did Stanko Vujanovic look like? You describe him for us, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: He had a beard. He's a tall person, taller than me. I would say -- I'm not really good at describing people. If I would see the picture, I would definitely say who it is, and I can't describe much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And can you describe Miro Vujovic for us, his height and the rest of it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: He's a petit person. About my size, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you noticed that the two of them were having a row with Mr. -- with Major Sljivancanin by the barracks.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: That was inside the barracks, yes. They had an argument over there as well as there were another couple of JNA officers present.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What were they arguing about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: I'm not very sure. I wasn't really close to hear what they were arguing about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And all this was happening at the barracks, and you describe the relationship of forces between then members of the TO, and you note that there were far more JNA soldiers; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That means that quite simply they could have sent the TO members packing.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: I would say so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But as you say, they did not do that but they allowed the buses with the people in them to move off. As your friend got to know later on, they were being transported somewhere else; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: Nobody stopped the buses, no. No. They left in -- accompanied by military vehicles, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, you say that you went to Ovcara, you and Zoric, and that you saw the buses parked there and that you once again saw Major Sljivancanin there, and Vujanovic and Vujovic. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you sure you saw Sljivancanin up there again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: I'm hundred per cent sure. I even greeted him. He wouldn't reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And Zoric and these other people, how many of them were you able to take out of the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: Zoric tried about 15 people. I don't know how many he managed to take because he was coming and going. I managed to take two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you stopped doing that and Zoric told you to go to Petrova Gora - I assume that's a street or district in Vukovar - for him to be able to tell his wife to get dinner ready for all the people that he was going to save; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you went back to Ovcara and it was dark by that time; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: It wasn't really dark over there yet, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you saw Vujovic and Vujanovic issuing orders, and in your opinion, it was quite obvious that the two of them, as you said, were the main two people there in that locality of Ovcara; right? Was that how you saw it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: They are the only two people that, well, basically in higher ranks that I saw inside the hangar. I didn't see any more -- anybody from the JNA anywhere outside or inside the hangar. And I didn't see them actually giving any kind of orders to anybody at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And Major Sljivancanin wasn't up there at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: No, no. At that time, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me just clarify that. Did you see Sljivancanin at Ovcara or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And whereabouts did you see him at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Outside the hanger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Outside the hanger.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But you didn't see anyone from the JNA inside the hangar; is that the point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what happened afterwards happened quite a long time after you had seen Sljivancanin; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: Would you mind clarifying the question? Like, in what sense?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You had seen Sljivancanin earlier on, and later on when you went back when it was dark, he wasn't there any more nor were there any members of the JNA in that hangar; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: That's correct, he wasn't there, but there were JNA soldiers still outside, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you sure they were JNA soldiers or might they have been the territorials of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: I would saw JNA soldiers because they were regular soldiers. They were based over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many of those soldiers were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: I don't recall the exact number, how many, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that in Ovcara you saw some soldiers who were not members of the JNA, and you even saw a woman among them; right? She couldn't have been a member of the JNA either.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: I don't recall saying that, no. No. She was a prisoner inside the hangar. I didn't say that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you said that there were no JNA members in the hangar itself.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, as you saw all this, you asked permission to leave Vukovar in order to visit your parents in Bijeljina. That's what you say in paragraph 46.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you tabled a request to that effect, and without any problems --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- you were given these documents; right? Now, in view of the fact that you were brought to Vukovar against your own free will, as you said, why didn't you ask previously that they allow you to leave Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: No one was allowed to leave Vukovar during the war. Only some exceptions were people that I guess were in power, but during the war, no one was allowed, and I was afraid to ask for any kind of stuff like that. But after the war, they were issuing a lot of -- a lot of papers, basically, to let you go. You could go for a couple of days and come back, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In the meantime, you learned that the people who were at Ovcara had been killed; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who did you hear that from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: People were saying in the streets. It was a rumour going on everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And since you heard people talking about that in the streets, did you happen to hear who had been responsible for doing the act?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: No, sir. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As I can see, you stayed on in Vukovar for a full six years afterwards, and as you yourself said, you kept hiding from people because you had saved these unfortunate people from Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you perhaps remember the names of the people you saved at Velepromet --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-006
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
